spd_hint: HPS (with MV/MH remnants; minority LED, CCT unknown)
notes: Ownership: Oncor owns 72,378 streetlights; City/TxDOT 23,303 (Vision Zero council briefing, Mar 2024). NBC DFW (29 Mar 2022): ~95,000 total, ~10,000 (just over 1 in 10) LED; <1 in 20 Oncor lights LED; ~15,000 city-owned of which nearly half LED; Oncor replacing mercury vapor/HPS with LED only on failure, new Oncor installs then still HPS or MH; 5-7 yr conversion horizon. Council item 24-118 (agenda 28 Feb 2024) authorised Oncor to replace non-working Oncor fixtures with LED (replace-on-failure program) — used as retrofit_start; no completion found. led_share_pct=10 is for 2022; by 2026 likely higher but no figure found. cct_k=2000 is nominal HPS, not a spec. Oncor tariff (rev. 22, eff. 1 Jun 2026) mentions a 'Company's standard installation' colour temperature but does NOT state the Kelvin value; customers pay extra for a different CCT. No Dallas/Oncor LED CCT found in any document — LED portion CCT unknown (era rule would suggest 3000-4000K).

Ownership: streetlights are 'installed, owned, and maintained by CenterPoint Energy' (Houston Public Works Street Light Request Application); city standard is LED 'white in color', 45 W residential, 95/115 W collector/thoroughfare. 2014 City-CenterPoint agreement to convert ~165,000 HPS/MV/MH to LED over ~3 years (C40); 35,000 done by Oct 2015 (C40); >60,000 of ~176,000 by Mar 2016 (Kinder Institute). CenterPoint web page (search snippet only; page 403) says ~400,000 HPS converted to LED across Greater Houston — no completion date documented, so retrofit_end blank and led_share null, but LED is almost certainly dominant. CCT: 4000K is supported only by press/petition context — Houston Chronicle 'Are LED street lights a bright idea?' (seen in search snippet only; page did not load) refers to 'the current 4000K', and a Jan 2016 change.org petition update argues against '4000K as a national standard'; Mayor Turner asked CenterPoint/Public Works to cost a change, CenterPoint said switching would be too costly (search snippet). No contract/tariff CCT found; no evidence of a mid-program switch to 3000K. Newer CenterPoint installs could be 3000K — unverified.

Ownership split: most streetlights in Miami/Miami-Dade are FPL-owned under FPL street-lighting tariffs (LT-1 for LED); Miami-Dade County (unincorporated areas, via Parks/special taxing districts) and municipalities own some; Homestead has its own utility. FPL LED program approved by Florida PSC Apr 2017 (retrofit_start). Florida Bulldog (Jul 2019): FPL had >125,000 LED streetlights statewide, ~20,000 in Miami-Dade, target >50,000 in Miami-Dade; County Commission voted 12-0 on 4 Jun 2019 to halt FPL LED installs in unincorporated areas over 'dark spots' pending audit. North Miami (FPL) conversion completed Nov 2018. CCT: not documented for Miami. Search snippets (not loaded) indicate FPL/Miami-Dade 'considered installing 4000K', a St. Augustine Beach FPL comparison titled '70 Watt HPS vs 26 Watt 4000K', and FDOT 2021 specs set 4000K max/default — suggests FPL's standard roadway LED is 4000K but this is unconfirmed for Miami. City of Miami-specific LED share not found. Treat as unknown; needs FPL LT-1 catalogue or City of Miami/County records.

Toronto is NOT yet converted. Ownership: Toronto Hydro has owned the streetlighting portfolio since 2006. Toronto Hydro 'Streetlighting Infrastructure Investment Report' (1 Apr 2026, City EX committee background file): ~109,900 cobrahead (HPS), ~33,500 acorn (metal halide), ~15,900 LED in service => LED ~10% of ~159,300. Acorns replaced with LED on failure since 2022; HPS cobraheads replaced with LED on failure since Q3 2023 (~4-5k/yr) — used as retrofit_start. Report explicitly states: HPS 'typically' ~2000K; legacy MH acorns 4000K; the cobrahead LED and acorn LED currently approved by Toronto Hydro are both 3000K (consistent with Toronto Public Health 2016 briefing note recommending <=3000K). New program (announced 2026): CAD 577M to convert all ~173,100 luminaires to LED with controls by end-2035, ~60% within five years. cct_k=2000 reflects dominant HPS stock (report's nominal value), not a spec; downtown/residential acorn areas are 4000K MH — so the stock is genuinely bimodal.

City-owned (Streets Dept / Philadelphia Energy Authority). Project FAQ: 'All lights on the project are a warm color temperature - 3000 Kelvin'; standard and 'boosted' (higher-lumen) fixtures share the same CCT. PEA release: completion celebrated 28 Oct 2025, all ~130,000 neighbourhood streetlights replaced one-to-one, on budget ($91.2M bond), with lighting management system. Earlier pre-project city LEDs were largely 4000K (Inquirer, search snippet only) but the one-to-one replacement of 'every neighborhood streetlight' implies these were replaced. led_share 100% refers to city neighbourhood streetlights; PennDOT highway lighting and private/decorative lights are outside the project.

City-owned (NYC DOT; ~396,572 lights of all types, ~250,000 standard cobraheads). Bloomberg announced (2013) all 250,000 standard fixtures to LED by 2017; conversion began Oct 2013. DOT page today: 'almost all' streetlights retrofitted (no % given, no completion date). CCT: Manhattan CB4 letter (7 Jun 2016) refers to 'the current 4,000 Kelvin lamps'; Urban Omnibus (2018): Brooklyn and Queens used standard 4000K. Brick Underground (3 Feb 2017) quotes a DOT rep saying the city would 'move forward in installing 3,000K LED street light fixtures' citing AMA recommendations — applied to Manhattan, the Bronx and Staten Island going forward, with no plan to replace installed 4000K in Brooklyn/Queens. By Sep 2017 DOT reported >60,000 LED in Brooklyn, 81,000 Queens, 33,000 Bronx, 22,000 Manhattan, 31,000 Staten Island (pr17-066) — so Brooklyn+Queens (~141k, 4000K) plus pre-2017 Bronx/SI installs are 4000K; remaining Manhattan and later installs 3000K. Net: 4000K-dominant, 3000K minority. Earlier 78 W units replaced by 64 W after complaints (a wattage change, not CCT). A City Council bill to cap LED streetlights at 3000K (introduced Jun 2015) was reported stalled in committee (search snippet); the switch was a DOT policy, not law. Bronx/SI split between 4000K and 3000K not quantified.

City-owned (Public Works Street Lighting Division). Starting stock 2010: 64,000 electric lights = 42,000 mercury vapour + 22,000 HPS (Commissioner Massaro, DOE/MSSLC 2012 slides); plus ~2,800 gas lamps. LED conversion began fall 2010 (MV cobraheads first, 2,800 residential then 12,000 more), continued to MV acorns/rectilinear from fall 2012; 38,838 of 64,000 LED by 26 Sep 2014 (city/Analyze Boston, search snippet). Boston Globe (22 Sep 2022): ~80,000 lights total, ~14,000 still conventional electric plus 2,800 gas => ~79% LED (derived; boston.gov page says 71,000 total, so % is approximate); Wu administration/Ameresco audit (2022-23) to convert the remainder incl. gas lamps to LED. CCT: no Boston document found stating Kelvin. The 2010-2014 wave predates the AMA 2016 guidance; the era rule gives ~4000K, and one secondary web source (search snippet) lists Boston among cities with 4000K LED. Some 2010-11 first-generation fixtures may be >4000K. Remaining conversions (post-2022) likely 3000K or lower but unverified. Treat cct as inferred.

City-owned (Street Transportation Dept.), contractor Ameresco. CORRECTION to prior assumption: Phoenix chose 2700K, not 3000K. City of Phoenix official agency post: ~100,000 street lights converted to 'a 2,700 kelvin LED fixture - the city's new kelvin standard for street lights'; work began 27 Nov 2017, zone-by-zone, programmed to finish fall 2019; no arterial/residential CCT split. Completion announced by Ameresco 14 Jan 2020 (BusinessWire page 403 — seen via search snippet) and KTAR 15 Jan 2020 ('new street lights are 2,700 Kelvins'). Council approved after 'several years of testing' and a public health debate (2017). retrofit_end set to 2019-12 (completion announced Jan 2020). led_share 100% refers to the ~100,000 standard roadway lights; decorative/pre-program pilot fixtures not characterised.

Ownership/operation: Georgia Power now maintains and services all streetlights in City of Atlanta right-of-way (ATLDOT; maintenance transferred May 2022 after a critical audit); ~60,000 streetlights (inside.lighting 2022). 'One Atlanta - Light Up the Night' (announced 29 Jun 2021): Georgia Power to add 10,000 (later 20,000) LED lights and upgrade existing lights to LED; ATLDOT draft release (Oct 2024): >17,000 upgraded/installed in phases 1-2, 15,000 of 20,000 in phase 3 — i.e. ~32,000 by late 2024, suggesting LED is now majority but no % documented. Georgia Power began statewide LED roadway conversions earlier (>50,000 LED of ~400,000 GP roadway lights by Nov 2015), so some Atlanta LEDs predate 2021. CCT: no Atlanta or Georgia Power tariff (OLG-15 checked) document states Kelvin. Georgia Power offered 3000K by 2016 (Decatur waited for 3000K fixtures, AJC Oct 2016: Decatur LEDs 3000K), implying 4000K was the earlier product. A June 2017 Atlanta change.org petition complains of 'cool/blue' light (no K stated). Hence 4000K (pre-2016/17) + likely 3000K (LUTN era) mixed — unverified.

Ownership split: SOBSE (city Secretaría de Obras y Servicios) runs the primary road network lighting; the 16 alcaldías run secondary/local streets — so stock is heterogeneous. SOBSE bulletin 045/2023 (30 Jan 2023): 46% of luminaires migrated to LED 2019-2022, target 55% in 2023; 123,516 LED luminaires lighting the city; 30,800 new luminaires in previously dark areas; 'Senderos Seguros' 710 km. Unclear whether 46% refers to SOBSE-managed network or whole city (no total count found). Continued LED programs under Brugada (e.g. 1,900+ LED luminaires in colonia Álamos, Sep 2025; 'Ciudad Iluminada' contracts across alcaldías, search snippet). Legacy technology presumed HPS (vapor de sodio) — not explicitly stated in documents loaded. NOM-031-ENER-2019 regulates LED luminaire efficacy/CRI but not CCT. No CCT found in any SOBSE bulletin or press item loaded. Needs SOBSE licitación annexes (CompraNet) for Kelvin.
